note: Approved demonstration prompts. 'evidence' distinguishes an example that is answered from verified project documentation or a live backend call ('verified') from one that is a clearly labelled teaching illustration ('illustrative'). Illustrative examples are never presented as legal output, and no example stages a fake search, citation or prediction.

examples.title: What VIDHIVEDA does and how to use it
examples.prompt: What is VIDHIVEDA, and how should I use it?
examples.learning_objective: See the project explain its own purpose, the real workflow, the features that exist, and the limits it holds itself to.
expected: States the purpose: legal research over an indexed Indian case-law corpus, with a visible source trail.
Describes the actual workflow from the Research tab through retrieved records, the reading view and citation verification.
Lists features that exist in this build (Research, Compare, Knowledge, Statutes & Articles, Documents, Settings).
States the limits: 100 judgment PDFs, no legal advice, no outcome prediction.
Offers a next action that opens a real feature.

examples.title: Explain RAG in plain language
examples.prompt: Explain how VIDHIVEDA uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation in simple language.
examples.learning_objective: Understand retrieval-first design: what is retrieved, what the language model is allowed to do with it, and why a citation is checkable.
expected: Explains retrieval first, generation second.
Names the real components: query analysis, embeddings with sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, ChromaDB collection vidhiveda_legal_cases, optional reranking, generation, citation verification.
Explains that retrieved chunks are supplied to the model as numbered SOURCE blocks and that the prompt forbids inventing cases, citations, statutes and dates.
Explains the source references are chunk ids that can be fetched back.
States clearly that retrieval similarity does not guarantee legal correctness.

examples.title: Submitting a query and reviewing judgments
examples.prompt: How can I submit a legal query and review relevant judgments?
examples.learning_objective: Learn the research workflow end to end, including which fields matter and what to do when nothing is found.
expected: Walks through the Research tab step by step.
Names the required input (the query, minimum 2 characters) and the optional Court and Year filters.
Explains how results are displayed: case name, court/year, stored passage, chunk id, source filename, similarity.
Explains that citations are listed separately and verified against retrieved chunks.
Explains the 'no results' path: broaden the query, clear filters, or accept that the topic is outside the corpus.
examples.notes: This is a guidance example. It explains and links to the research interface; it does not itself search the legal corpus.

examples.title: Comparing two opposing arguments (illustrative)
examples.prompt: Show me how VIDHIVEDA can compare two opposing arguments in a hypothetical contract dispute.
examples.learning_objective: See how a two-sided comparison is structured, and how the system keeps facts, assumptions and missing information apart.
expected: Explains the Compare tab inputs: legal issue (required), case facts, provisions, and one position per side.
Identifies the legal issues that would need researching in a contract dispute.
Explains that supporting and contrary precedents are both reviewed, with precedents grouped by source document.
Explains how the comparison separates established facts, stated assumptions and missing information.
States that any assessment must be grounded in actually retrieved authorities, and that evidence quality is reported as sufficient, limited or insufficient.
examples.illustrative_notice: Illustrative educational example. No real judgment, case number, quotation or citation is invented, and no side is declared the winner.

examples.title: How an outcome estimate would work
examples.prompt: How would VIDHIVEDA estimate a possible case outcome?
examples.learning_objective: Learn why the prediction capability is honestly unavailable, and how it would have to be built and validated.
expected: Checks the live model status rather than assuming one state, because the trained artifact is not committed and environments differ.
If no artifact is present: states that no prediction is produced and quotes the reason the API gives.
If an experimental classifier is loaded: reports its version, calibration and the recorded held-out metrics, and explains why a very small test partition makes it experimental.
Distinguishes the supervised classifier (which produces the label and calibrated probability) from the LLM (which only explains retrieved authorities in prose).
Explains the validation a prediction would need: pre-judgment features to avoid verdict leakage, a temporal split, calibration, and accuracy reported on unseen data.
Clarifies that the system supports legal research and does not make judicial decisions.
examples.notes: Demonstrates honest disclosure: the answer reports the live capability state — including the experimental caveat — instead of inventing or overstating a prediction.

examples.title: Legal search returned no results
examples.prompt: The legal search returned no results. What should I do?
examples.learning_objective: Practise a structured troubleshooting flow: meaning, causes, safe steps, whether retrying helps, and when to escalate.
expected: Explains what 'no results' means: retrieval ran and nothing matched closely enough with the current filters.
Lists likely causes, including a narrow Court or Year filter and a topic outside the 100-document corpus.
Suggests refining the query, clearing filters, and trying the legal principle or the statutory provision instead of the exact facts.
States whether retrying is appropriate: yes, with a changed query or cleared filters.
Says when to contact the administrator, and what to include.

examples.title: Which features are implemented
examples.prompt: Which features of VIDHIVEDA are currently implemented?
examples.learning_objective: Check the capability registry: what is implemented, what is partial or experimental, and what is deliberately unavailable.
expected: Returns the real status registry, grouped by status label.

Distinguishes implemented (research, citations, reading view, comparison, knowledge bundle, settings, voice input, support assistant, examples, troubleshooting, status, feedback) from partial, experimental and not_available entries.
Names the deliberate gaps: outcome prediction, area-of-law filter, persistent conversation history, statute full text.
Never presents a planned or unavailable capability as working.
examples.notes: Answered from backend/support/features.json, the maintained capability registry.

examples.title: Using the microphone
examples.prompt: How can I use voice input to ask a question?
examples.learning_objective: Learn the dictation workflow, its browser requirements, and its privacy caveat.
expected: Points at the microphone button inside the research search bar and explains the listening state.
Explains that browser microphone permission is required and that the page must be served over https or localhost.
Explains that the transcript fills the same input for review and is never auto-submitted, and that typed input always remains available.
States plainly that the feature is unavailable in browsers without the Web Speech API.
Notes that browser speech recognition may use the browser vendor's cloud service.

examples.title: Dark mode and light mode
examples.prompt: How do I switch between dark mode and light mode?
examples.learning_objective: Find the appearance controls and understand that the reader has its own independent theme.
expected: Points to Settings, then Appearance & personalization.
Names the three interface modes: Light, Dark and System default.
Mentions the palette gallery and the custom three-colour palette, which restyle the interface through theme tokens.
Notes the reading view has its own light/sepia/dark theme controlled separately.
Discloses that a control which is not there is not implemented, instead of inventing one.

examples.title: Is a response supported by a judgment?
examples.prompt: How do I know whether a response is supported by a judgment?
examples.learning_objective: Understand the difference between retrieved source material and generated summary, and how to verify a citation yourself.
expected: Explains how to open a cited record in the reading view to read the stored passage.
Explains the direct verification path: GET /api/research/chunk/{chunk_id} returns the exact stored row.
Distinguishes retrieved source material from generated prose, and names the answer-source label that tells them apart.
States that a citation must be verified against the original document and that similarity is not correctness.
Explains that a verified citation does not by itself prove the passage supports the proposition.
